title: The Great Depression
summary: Trace how one economic collapse sent shockwaves through four systems — political, economic, social-cultural, and geographic-environmental — and decide which change lasted longest.
challenge: The 1929 crash did more than empty bank accounts. Its shockwaves reshaped American politics, the economy, society and culture, and even the land itself. Follow the event outward through four systems, weigh who benefited and who bore the costs, and decide which change left the deepest mark.

paths.immediateKey: Voters reject Hoover's approach; FDR and the Democrats sweep the 1932 election.
paths.secondaryKey: A lasting expansion of the federal government's role in the economy and social welfare; a new Democratic coalition.
paths.evidenceKey: New Deal laws (Emergency Banking Act, Social Security Act); FDR's fireside chats; growth of federal agencies.

paths.immediateKey: Waves of bank failures, collapsing credit, ~25% unemployment, and a ~30% drop in output.
paths.secondaryKey: New federal financial regulation and safety nets to prevent a recurrence.
paths.evidenceKey: FDIC (1933), SEC (1934), Social Security (1935); Federal Reserve data on bank suspensions and the money supply.

paths.immediateKey: Widespread poverty, homelessness ('Hoovervilles'), and breadlines; repatriation pressure on people of Mexican heritage.
paths.secondaryKey: A strengthened labor movement and a documentary and protest culture.
paths.evidenceKey: FSA photographs (Dorothea Lange's Migrant Mother); Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath (1939); WPA arts projects.

paths.immediateKey: The Dust Bowl — drought, over-plowing, and dust storms ruin southern Plains farmland.
paths.secondaryKey: Mass 'Okie' migration to California and new federal soil-conservation policy.
paths.evidenceKey: The Soil Conservation Service (1935); FSA migration photos and California migrant-camp records.

mapData.benefitedKey: Depositors and investors gained lasting protections (FDIC/SEC); the elderly, unemployed, and unionized workers gained a permanent safety net; jobless workers got jobs through the WPA and CCC.
mapData.costKey: Displaced farmers and Dust Bowl migrants; unemployed industrial and Black workers (last hired, first fired); Mexican Americans targeted by repatriation; uninsured depositors of banks that failed before 1933.
mapData.greatestKey: Which pathway — political, economic, social-cultural, or geographic-environmental — produced the most lasting change in American life? Use specific evidence to defend your ranking.

sources.titleKey: The Great Depression — Federal Reserve History
sources.descKey: How bank failures and a shrinking money supply deepened the collapse.
questionKeys: What role did bank failures and the Federal Reserve play?
How does this source explain the depth of the Depression?

sources.titleKey: Farm Security Administration / OWI Photographs — Library of Congress
sources.descKey: Government photographs documenting Dust Bowl migrants and rural poverty.
questionKeys: What do the photographs show about who bore the costs?
How do images shape the way we remember an era?

sources.titleKey: Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library & Museum (National Archives)
sources.descKey: FDR's fireside chats and New Deal records documenting the federal response.
questionKeys: How did FDR explain his response to the public?
Which New Deal program seems most consequential? Why?

comparePromptKeys: Compare your four pathways with a partner. Did you find the same immediate and secondary effects?
Did you rank the same pathway as most lasting? Defend your ranking with evidence.
conclusionKey: Which system's change lasted longest after the Great Depression? Support your ranking with specific evidence from at least two pathways and two sources.

ace.articulateKey: Summarize how the Great Depression affected one system in your own words.
ace.connectKey: Connect an immediate effect in one pathway to a secondary effect that still shapes life today.
ace.extendKey: Apply the 'shockwave through systems' idea to a more recent crisis, such as a recession or pandemic.

teacherText.keyideas: A single economic collapse produced systemic change across government (the New Deal and a larger federal role), the economy (regulation and safety nets that endure), society and culture (labor's rise; documentary art), and the environment (the Dust Bowl and soil conservation). The costs and benefits were unevenly distributed. Push students to rank effects with evidence, not to find one 'right' answer.
teacherText.misconceptions:
• The New Deal did not fully end the Depression; WWII mobilization drove full recovery.
• The Dust Bowl was worsened by farming practices, not drought alone.
• Recovery was uneven — many groups were excluded from New Deal gains.
teacherText.vocabulary: Great Depression, New Deal, FDIC, SEC, Social Security, Dust Bowl, repatriation, WPA/CCC, laissez-faire.
teacherText.context: Crash Oct. 1929; ~9,000 banks suspended 1930–33; unemployment ~25% by 1933; FDR elected 1932; New Deal from 1933; Dust Bowl mid-1930s ('Black Sunday' April 14, 1935).
